attempts_detail.primary_asr_text: On the train, I open the For You page and see my followed topics. I have only the ride to catch up, so I do not want to sort through unrelated stories. Google News uses topics and sources I follow. It can also use my past activity on Google services and YouTube. I can follow or unfollow topics, ask for more or less, and hide a source. These controls make the feed feel partly mine. I still worry an important story could be left out, but this quick start protects my morning time.

attempts_detail.primary_asr_text: Each time I scroll, I see familiar arguments and sources. I begin to wonder about stories outside that circle. I want to know why one article comes before another, but I cannot see all the signals behind the order or how much control I have over the recommendations. Clicks, likes, shares, and search history can shape what appears. The service may also be tuned for engagement and advertising income. That makes me uneasy. A hidden order may be choosing what I notice first. I want to protect my chance to meet views I would not normally open.

attempts_detail.primary_asr_text: Both readers want the same thing: the feed shapes what they understand. Neither is wrong to care about that, but they protect different stakes. One wants a manageable morning and control; the other wants views outside the usual feed. The first can follow, hide, or change display levels; the second cannot reach the ranking rules, which may shape the view without showing how. This is an uneven process, not two equal controls.

attempts_detail.primary_asr_text: The deeper question is not simply whether personalization helps or harms, it is who can shape the path to news and who can see that path. A feed may feel personal because it answers to a reader's choices, while part of the decision stays out of view. That boundary is the real tension.
